query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a ~10 at% Mo substitution into a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated‐temperature mechanical properties by inducing fine, thermally stable Mo‐rich precipitates that hinder dislocation movement and grain boundary sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy formulated with five or more elements (each in the 5–35 at% range) with Ti and Ni as the dominant constituents and without significant refractory element content.
generation.intervention: Substitute approximately 10 at% of one of the minor elements in the alloy composition with molybdenum (Mo).
generation.conditions: Testing and service conditions at elevated temperatures (approximately 800–1000 °C) under a controlled atmosphere that simulates extreme environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The targeted formation of a dispersed network of fine, Mo-rich precipitates or intermetallic phases within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The fine refractory precipitates produced by Mo addition provide precipitation strengthening by pinning dislocations and stabilizing grain boundaries, thereby reducing creep and maintaining yield strength at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-doped alloy is expected to show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the baseline Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy without Mo.
generation.baseline: The original Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy composition lacking any Mo addition.
generation.boundary: Valid for compositions maintaining high-entropy criteria (each element between 5–35 at%), with Mo addition kept within about 5–10 at% substitution and testing in the 800–1000 °C temperature range. Results are assumed to be applicable provided that the microstructure remains stable without forming deleterious phases.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in yield strength and creep resistance are not yet determined; phase stability and precipitate morphology under prolonged exposure require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with the baseline Ti–Ni primary composition and the other with 10 at% Mo substitution replacing one minor element. Subject all samples to identical thermomechanical processing to ensure comparable starting microstructures. Perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests at 800–1000 °C and utilize transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize precipitate formation and distribution.
measurements: Creep rate under controlled load conditions
Microstructural analysis of precipitate presence and morphology (via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength and/or creep resistance relative to the baseline alloy, or if TEM analysis fails to confirm the presence of fine, stable Mo-rich precipitates under the testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
